title: Region Selection Can Reverse Apparent Spectral Contrast in Optical Diffraction Tomography
content: Spectral differences between optical diffraction tomography (ODT) reconstructions are commonly summarized as a mean over a region of interest drawn from the reconstructions themselves. Here we show that the rule used to draw that region can decide the sign of the summary. We reanalyzed the public reconstructions of a two-photon-polymerized scattering microphantom imaged at 633 and 835 nm, using both the Gerchberg–Papoulis support-constrained (GPSC) and the electric-field multislice beam-propagation (MSBP-E) volumes deposited with the original study. For GPSC at a contrast threshold of 0.007, the mean 633 − 835 nm difference was −0.34 × 10⁻³ RI over voxels exceeding the threshold at both wavelengths and +0.77 × 10⁻³ RI over voxels exceeding it at either wavelength. An exact partition of the union traced the reversal to voxels selected at only one wavelength, which made up 71% of the union; giving them 0.115 of the per-voxel weight of shared voxels was enough to bring the mean to zero. In MSBP-E both means were positive (+1.14 and +1.25 × 10⁻³ RI) across six thresholds and eight translations, yet a differential reference offset of +0.001 RI reduced the union mean to 0.008 × 10⁻³ RI. The sign of a region-averaged spectral contrast is therefore neither reconstruction-invariant nor robust to the numerical reference, and on its own it cannot indicate material dispersion.
